messages.content: I wrote a little polling loop with a bare `except:` around it so it would 'never crash', and now Ctrl-C doesn't stop it anymore. The program just keeps running. What did the bare except do?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
A: bare except caught it - the Ctrl-C vanished
B: escaped 'except Exception', landed in BaseException: KeyboardInterrupt

The bare `except:` caught your Ctrl-C and threw it away. `KeyboardInterrupt` does not derive from `Exception` - it derives directly from `BaseException`, alongside `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit`. That split is deliberate: those three are control signals from the interpreter or the user, not failures in your data.

A bare `except:` is shorthand for `except BaseException:`, so it catches all three. Your loop 'never crashes' because it also never obeys - the interrupt was raised, your handler silently consumed it, and execution continued as if nothing happened. Version B shows the fix: `except Exception` lets the interrupt pass straight through to the `BaseException` handler, which is where a deliberate shutdown path belongs if you want one at all.

Rule of thumb: the broadest catch in ordinary code is `except Exception`. Go wider only at a program's outermost edge, and even there, re-raise or exit after logging - never just continue.
My dashboard printed 'revenue: 0' all morning and no error anywhere. When I finally removed the bare except around the revenue call, it exploded immediately. Why did the bare version fail so quietly?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
bare except version -> revenue: 0
narrowed version -> AttributeError: 'Report' object has no attribute 'totals'

Your typo - `report.totals()` instead of `report.total()` - raised `AttributeError` the very first time it ran. The bare `except:` caught it, because a bare except catches *everything*, and your handler's fallback of 0 turned a programming bug into a plausible-looking number. Zero revenue is a value a dashboard can display without complaint, so the bug wore a disguise for hours.

The narrowed version only promises to handle `ValueError`. An `AttributeError` is not the failure that handler exists for, so it propagates and you see the real message: `'Report' object has no attribute 'totals'`. That is the whole discipline: a handler should name the failures it knows how to recover from. Everything else is either a different failure (let it reach a handler that knows it) or a bug (let it crash loudly during development).

A fallback value deserves extra suspicion. Returning 0, an empty list, or a default on *any* error converts crashes into wrong answers, and wrong answers are much harder to notice than crashes.
I keep reading 'never catch BaseException, catch Exception instead'. What actually lives outside Exception, and why does the distinction matter in practice?

Three built-in exceptions derive from `BaseException` without going through `Exception`:

- `KeyboardInterrupt` - the user pressed Ctrl-C and is asking the program to stop.
- `SystemExit` - something called `sys.exit()`; the exception carries the exit code and is how Python normally ends a program.
- `GeneratorExit` - raised inside a generator when it is closed early, so it can run cleanup.

They are control signals, not data failures. `ValueError`, `KeyError`, `OSError` and everything your code ordinarily raises sit under `Exception`, so `except Exception` catches all of the failures while letting the control signals do their job.

Why it matters: a handler that catches `BaseException` (which is what a bare `except:` does) will swallow Ctrl-C and keep running, and will intercept `sys.exit()` so exit codes never reach the shell - scripts that 'succeed' after being told to die break pipelines and schedulers that depend on those codes. The one legitimate place to catch `BaseException` is a top-level supervisor that logs the interruption and then re-raises it. Catching it and carrying on is the part that's never right.

My loader reads amount lines from a file. Some lines are junk and should just be skipped, but I also don't want real bugs in the averaging step to get quietly swallowed by the same handler. How do I split which errors get caught where?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
load: skipped bad line 'oops'
load: kept [10, 20, 30]
average: 20.0
summarize let it propagate: TypeError - unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'NoneType'

Each error is caught at the level that actually knows what to do about it. A junk line is a *known* condition of the input file, and `load_amounts` is the level that knows the policy - skip it and note it - so the `ValueError` handler lives there, wrapped tightly around just the parse call.

`summarize` has no handler at all, on purpose. When a `None` slips into its list, `sum` raises `TypeError`, and there is nothing sensible summarize could do to recover - inventing a number would be worse than crashing. So the error propagates to the caller, who learns there is an upstream bug, with the message naming the real problem: an `int` met a `NoneType`.

The pattern to copy: handle an exception where you can take a meaningful action (skip, default, retry, translate). If a function cannot do any of those for an error, it should not catch it - catching without a recovery action only strips information from the traceback and delays the diagnosis.

My error log keeps saying 'fetch failed' but the network is fine. Here's the shape of the code:

```python
try:
    page = fetch(url)
    title = page['title']
    save(title)
except Exception:
    log('fetch failed')
```

Why is the log lying to me?

The log is lying because the `try` block covers three operations and the handler blames all of them on the first one. Only `fetch(url)` can fail because of the network. If the page comes back without a `'title'` key, `page['title']` raises `KeyError`; if the database is locked, `save` raises too - and both get logged as 'fetch failed', sending you to debug a healthy network.

Shrink the `try` to the one call whose failure the handler actually understands:

```python
try:
    page = fetch(url)
except FetchError:
    log('fetch failed')
    return
title = page['title']
save(title)
```

Python even gives you the `else` clause for exactly this shape - code in `else:` runs only when the `try` body succeeded, and its exceptions are *not* caught by the handlers above it. The discipline is: a `try` block should contain the risky call and as little else as possible, so that when a handler fires you know precisely which operation failed and the handler's story about it is true.

A pricing helper returns 0 both when an item genuinely isn't in the price table and in some other situation I haven't pinned down. I suspect the broad except is covering for a bug. Can you show me how that happens?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
missing item, broad: 0
missing item, narrow: 0
broken table, broad: 0
broken table, narrow -> TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable

There it is, in the third line: when `table` is `None` - a bug somewhere upstream - the broad version returns 0, exactly the same answer it gives for a legitimately missing item. Two completely different situations (item not priced yet vs. the price table never loaded) collapse into one indistinguishable output, so the bug has been silently masquerading as 'unpriced item' every time it fired.

The narrow version promises to handle only the known condition, `KeyError`, and keeps that promise for both missing items. But the `None` table raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`, which the handler doesn't claim, so it propagates and announces the real problem.

When you inherit a broad handler, this is the audit to run: list every exception the guarded code can actually raise, and ask which of them the fallback is *correct* for. Usually the honest answer is one or two types. Name those, and let the rest be loud.

My config loader handles a missing file by falling back to defaults, which works. But when the file exists and the process can't read it, the fallback doesn't trigger and the program dies with a traceback. Both are file problems - why does one handler not cover both?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
missing.ini -> no handler fired except FileNotFoundError: using defaults
locked.ini -> PermissionError needed its OWN handler (errno 13)

`FileNotFoundError` and `PermissionError` are siblings, not parent and child - both derive from `OSError`, but neither derives from the other. An `except FileNotFoundError` clause matches only that type (and its subclasses), so the permission failure passes straight by it.

That separation is a feature. 'File not there yet' is a normal first-run condition and defaults are a reasonable answer. 'File exists but you may not read it' is an environment problem a human should hear about - silently running on defaults would hide a deployment mistake behind plausible behavior. The two deserve different responses, so they get different handlers.

If you ever do want one handler for all file trouble, `except OSError` catches the whole family - but then check which one you got before choosing a response, because the right recovery differs per member.
I have both an `except Exception` and an `except ValueError` on the same try, and I'm fairly sure the ValueError one never runs. Is Python just picking the first match?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
wrong order: generic handler ran
right order: specific handler ran

Exactly that: Python tests the `except` clauses top to bottom and runs the *first* one whose type matches. Since `ValueError` is a subclass of `Exception`, the generic clause matches first and the specific clause below it is dead code - Python will not warn you about this; it is perfectly legal, just unreachable.

The rule is to order handlers from most specific to most general, as in the second function: `ValueError` gets its chance before the `Exception` safety net. The same trap exists anywhere types are related by inheritance - `except OSError` above `except FileNotFoundError` shadows the file-not-found handler the same way.

A useful smell test: if you swap two adjacent handlers and behavior cannot change, one of them was unreachable. Linters (pylint's `bad-except-order`) can flag this, but the habit of reading handler lists as a cascade, most-specific-first, prevents it.

You've told me to catch narrowly, but my job runner has `except Exception` at the top of its loop that processes queued jobs one by one. If I narrow it, one weird job kills the whole runner. Is the broad catch there actually wrong?

No - that is one of the places a broad catch is the *correct* design, and the difference is responsibility. Your loop sits at a boundary: it owns the decision of what a failed job means. If the handler logs the full traceback, marks that one job as failed so it isn't silently lost, and moves on to the next job, then the broad catch isn't hiding anything - it's a supervisor doing its job. One poisoned job shouldn't take down the forty healthy ones behind it.

The same catch would be wrong in the middle of a library function, because there the code *cannot* take responsibility: it doesn't know whether the caller would rather retry, abort, or substitute a default, and swallowing the error just steals the caller's choice.

So the rules for a legitimate broad catch at a boundary are: catch `Exception`, not `BaseException`, so Ctrl-C and `sys.exit()` still work; log the complete traceback, not just the message; record the failure somewhere durable (a failed-jobs table, a dead-letter queue), because a log nobody reads is a silent failure with extra steps; and never let the handler itself be the last word on data - the job is marked failed, not marked done. Meet those, and the broad catch is engineering, not laziness.

A record processor divides by a quantity field, and when that's zero the error handler tries to log the record id - but support says the error they see mentions an id, not a division. It feels like the handler is replacing the real error. Is that possible?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
what the caller sees: ValueError - invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'x-9'
the original error, demoted to __context__: ZeroDivisionError

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
handler: qty was 0 for record x-9 - returning None
result: None

Entirely possible, and it's what your code does. The division raises `ZeroDivisionError`; the handler runs `int("x-9")`, which raises `ValueError`. The new exception is the one that propagates - the caller sees a complaint about an id, exactly as support reported. The original `ZeroDivisionError` survives only as the `__context__` ('During handling of the above exception...') in the traceback, which is the part of the report everyone stops reading.

Handlers are code, and code in a handler runs at the worst possible moment - something already went wrong, so the data and state around it are suspect. Anything a handler does that can itself fail (parsing, formatting, I/O) is a candidate mask. The second run shows the repair: the handler treats the id as opaque text and does no conversion at all, so nothing in the handler can throw and the recovery (returning None, with a note naming the record) is the only outcome.
When my port parser fails, the log just says 'ValueError' and I have to guess which input caused it and whether it was even the same kind of failure. How should the raise sites be written?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
8080 -> 8080
eighty -> ValueError: port must be a whole number, got 'eighty'
99999 -> ValueError: port must be between 1 and 65535, got 99999

Two different failures, two messages that each answer the three questions a reader actually has: what was expected, what was found, and (implicitly, from the value) where it came from. `'eighty'` fails the whole-number rule and the message quotes the offending text; `99999` parses fine but breaks the range rule, and its message names the range and the value. From the log line alone you can now tell a typo in a config file from an out-of-range assignment, without reproducing anything.

Two details worth copying. The `!r` in the f-string quotes the value, so an empty string or stray whitespace is visible instead of looking like a blank in the log. And each raise sits at the exact check that failed, raising immediately - the further a value travels from the check that rejected it, the more generic the message is forced to become.

Compare `ValueError` with no message at all: same exception type, zero information. The type is for the code that catches; the message is for the human who reads the log at 2 a.m. Write both deliberately.

My config loader wraps JSON errors in its own ConfigError so callers don't need to know about the json module. But now when the config is malformed I can't see the underlying parse problem anymore. How do I keep both?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
raised: ConfigError - config is not valid JSON
cause: JSONDecodeError - Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)
cause attached explicitly: True

`raise ... from e` gives you both layers. Callers catch `ConfigError` and never import the json module - the abstraction holds. But the original `JSONDecodeError` is attached as `__cause__`, and a traceback prints the whole story: the parse error first ('Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2'), then the line 'The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception', then your `ConfigError`.

The cause is usually the most diagnostic part of the whole report - it carries the line and column inside the file, which your wrapper's message can't know. Discarding it to keep the abstraction 'clean' trades a tidy catch clause for an undebuggable failure.

Note the difference from raising inside an `except` block with no `from`: that sets `__context__` implicitly and prints 'During handling of the above exception', which reads as an accident. `from e` says the wrapping was a decision. Same information preserved, clearer intent.

My helper converts a missing dict key into a ValueError with a clear message, but the traceback still shows the KeyError underneath and people keep asking about it. The KeyError adds nothing - the field name is already in my message. Can I make it stop showing?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
raised: missing required field: email
cause: None
context suppressed: True

`raise ... from None` is exactly that tool. It sets `__cause__` to None and flips `__suppress_context__` to True, so the traceback prints only your `ValueError` - the `KeyError: 'email'` frame, which merely restates what your message already says, disappears.

Contrast it with the chaining case: there, the JSON error carried a line and column that the wrapper's message couldn't know, so the cause was diagnostic gold and worth keeping. Here the cause is a pure echo. The rule isn't 'always chain' or 'always suppress' - it's to ask what the underlying exception adds. If it adds information (a position, an errno, a nested reason), chain it with `from e`. If it adds only noise, `from None` keeps the report readable.

One caution: suppress when you're confident the cause is an echo, not when you're merely tired of seeing it. A suppressed cause is gone from the record entirely; if there's any chance it held a clue, chain instead.
My find_user function needs a 'not found' outcome. Half my codebase returns None for it, half raises, and one older module returns -1. Which should it be, and why?

Pick based on how the caller is expected to treat 'not found' - but for a lookup like `find_user`, raising a dedicated `NotFound` exception (or returning None *consistently* if absence is routine) both beat the -1, which should go first: a sentinel integer is indistinguishable from data, is silently truthy/falsy in confusing ways (-1 is truthy in Python), and every caller must remember to check it. Forgotten checks turn into wrong behavior instead of errors.

The honest comparison of the other two:

- **Return None** when absence is a normal, expected outcome the caller will handle immediately - a cache probe, a `dict.get`. Its weakness is ambiguity: None can mean 'not found', 'found, and the value is None', or 'nobody looked'. Callers also forget the check and crash later with a `NoneType` error far from the lookup.
- **Raise** when absence breaks the caller's plan - the request names a user who must exist to proceed. The failure happens at the lookup, with the id in the message, and the caller who *can* handle absence catches one specific exception type at one place.

Whichever you choose, the real defect in your codebase is the mixture. Three conventions means every call site is a guessing game. Standardize per function by the question 'is absence part of this function's normal story?' - and document the choice in the name or docstring, e.g. `find_user` returns None, `get_user` raises.

Right now my shop code raises generic Exception with different message strings for 'out of stock' and 'card declined', and the checkout code string-matches the messages to decide what to show the customer. There's a better way, isn't there?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
pen -> tell the customer it is out of stock
pad -> ask for another card
sold mug

String-matching error messages is the fragility you're feeling: reword a message and the checkout silently breaks. Exception *types* are the stable contract. Here, `OutOfStock` and `PaymentDeclined` are distinct types, so the caller dispatches on what happened, not on how someone phrased it.

The shared base class earns its place too. Both derive from `ShopError`, so a different layer - say the top-level request handler - can catch `ShopError` once to log 'a shop operation failed' without knowing the subtypes, while the checkout catches the specific types to choose the customer's message. Specific handlers near the decision, general handler at the boundary: that's the hierarchy doing two jobs at two levels.

Keep the hierarchy shallow and meaningful. A new exception type is justified when some caller will *do something different* upon catching it - different message, different retry policy, different status code. If no caller will ever distinguish two errors, they don't need two types; one type with a good message is enough.

I wrapped a call like this so failures would be 'handled':

```python
try:
    data = read_sensor()
except OSError:
    raise OSError('error')
```

Now the logs show just 'error' with no filename or errno, and the traceback points at my handler instead of the real failure. What did I do wrong?

You didn't wrap the error - you replaced it. `raise OSError('error')` constructs a brand-new exception at the handler line, so everything the original carried is discarded: the errno, the filename the OS named, and the traceback showing where inside `read_sensor` things went wrong. The new traceback starts at your `raise`, which is why the logs point at the one line that isn't the problem.

If your handler only exists to add nothing, delete it and let the original propagate. If you caught it to do something on the way past (log, clean up, count) and then want the failure to continue, use a bare `raise` with no argument:

```python
try:
    data = read_sensor()
except OSError:
    log('sensor read failed')
    raise
```

The bare `raise` re-raises the *same* exception object with its original traceback intact. And when you genuinely need to translate the error into your own type, chain it - `raise SensorError('read failed') from e` - so the original stays attached as the cause instead of being erased. The pattern to unlearn is `raise SomeError('...')` inside an except block with no `from`: it's an information shredder.

I import order rows like 'pens,12' from a text file. When a quantity is junk, the error just says the int conversion failed - it doesn't say which row, so with a 900-row file I'm stuck hunting. How do I make the error carry the row?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
('pens', 12)
rejected: row 2: quantity 'six' is not a whole number
('mugs', 4)

The conversion happens at the one place that knows the row number, so that's where the error is re-raised - with the line number and the raw field baked into the message: `row 2: quantity 'six' is not a whole number`. Whoever reads the import log can go straight to line 2 of the file.

Notice what made this possible: the `int()` call was wrapped *at the parse site*, not by the caller. The caller only has the exception; by the time a generic handler up the stack sees it, the row number is unrecoverable unless the raise site put it in the message. Context decays with distance from the failure, so capture it at the failure.

The `from None` is deliberate here: the underlying message ('invalid literal for int()...') would only repeat what the new message says better. If the low-level error had added anything - a character position, say - you'd chain with `from e` instead.

My validation errors pack everything into the message string - field name, bad value, the limit it broke - and now the UI needs those pieces separately to highlight the right form field. Parsing them back out of the string feels wrong. What's the alternative?

It is wrong - a message string is a rendering, not a data structure. Put the pieces on the exception as attributes and let each consumer format what it needs:

```python
class FieldError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, field, value, rule):
        self.field = field
        self.value = value
        self.rule = rule
        super().__init__(f"{field}: {rule} (got {value!r})")
```

The UI catches `FieldError` and reads `e.field` to highlight the input and `e.rule` to pick its own wording, possibly in another language or tone. The log keeps the composed message, because `super().__init__` still built one. Neither consumer parses anything.

Two disciplines keep this clean. First, attributes are for the facts the exception *knows* - the field, the rejected value, the limit - not for presentation decisions like colors or full sentences aimed at one audience. Second, still always build the human message: tracebacks and logs show the message, not your attributes, and an exception whose printed form is empty will waste someone's night eventually.

Somewhere in my warehouse app, bin counts occasionally go negative, and by the time anyone notices, the trail is cold - nobody knows which bins or what the counts were. I want the audit step to stop the line the moment it sees an impossible state and preserve the evidence. How?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
audit stopped: bin 'A2' holds -3 units; snapshot: {'A1': 40, 'A2': -3, 'B1': 12}
clean audit total: 52

A negative bin count is not bad input - it's proof the program's own bookkeeping broke somewhere earlier. That's an invariant violation, and the right response is to stop immediately and raise, not to clamp the value to zero and continue with quietly falsified stock.

The raise carries a snapshot: the offending bin, its count, and the whole state at the moment of detection. Because dict ordering is insertion order, the snapshot prints exactly the state the audit saw. Whoever investigates starts from evidence instead of reconstructing the scene from memory - and because the check runs at audit time, the trail is minutes old, not days.

Two things make this pattern work. The check is cheap and sits on a path the data already flows through, so it runs constantly rather than in a monthly cleanup. And the exception is a dedicated type, `CorruptState`, so operations can alert on it specifically - this error means 'our code has a bug', a different page-the-human priority than 'a user typed something odd'.
Code review keeps bouncing my error messages as 'not helpful' but nobody will tell me what helpful actually looks like. Is there a formula?

There is a working formula - a good message answers three questions:

1. **What was expected?** The rule or shape that was required: 'port must be between 1 and 65535', 'expected a row of 4 columns'.
2. **What was found instead?** The actual value, quoted: "got 'eighty'", 'got 99999', 'found 3'. Quoting matters - with `repr` formatting, an empty string shows as `''` and stray spaces become visible instead of looking like a blank in the log.
3. **Where did it happen?** The identifier that locates the problem in the user's world: the row number, the field name, the filename, the account id. Not your function name - the reader can't act on that - but the coordinate in *their* data.

Watch the formula repair a useless message. Before: `raise ValueError('invalid input')` - none of the three questions answered. After: `raise ValueError(f"row 412: quantity must be a whole number, got 'six'")` - rule, value, and location all present.

One more test before you ship a message: could a person act on it without opening the source code? If they'd have to find you and ask what it means, it's not finished yet.

A sensor in my greenhouse takes a couple of seconds to wake up; the first read or two after boot just fails, then it answers fine. I want the code to ride over that instead of crashing the morning report. What does a sane retry look like here?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
attempt 1: ConnectionError - sensor not ready
attempt 2: ConnectionError - sensor not ready
attempt 3: success -> 21.5

This is the one case retry is *for*: the failure is transient - the world changes between attempts, because the sensor is waking up. Attempts 1 and 2 fail, attempt 3 succeeds, and the loop stops the moment it does.

Three features make this retry sane rather than hopeful. The catch is narrow - only `ConnectionError`, the known transient, is retried; a `ValueError` from a malformed reading would propagate immediately instead of being retried pointlessly. The loop is bounded (5 attempts), so a sensor that never wakes produces a failure, not an infinite loop. And each attempt is logged with its error, so the morning report's history shows the ride-over happened.

What this shape deliberately lacks is a delay - in real code you'd wait briefly between attempts, growing the wait each time. Retrying a waking or overloaded service in a tight loop can keep it from ever recovering; the pause is part of the politeness. But the structure - narrow catch, hard bound, stop on success - is the skeleton every retry should have.
I put a retry loop around a form-field parser because 'sometimes it fails'. It now takes five times longer to reject bad input and still rejects it. Why didn't retrying help at all?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
try 1: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
try 2: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
try 3: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
try 4: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
try 5: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
total tries for an input that can never parse: 5

Because nothing about the situation changes between tries. The input is the same string `'abc'`, the code is the same code, so the result is the same `ValueError`, five times in a row - the output is literally the identical line repeated. Retry is a bet that the failure is temporary: a waking sensor, a busy server, a dropped packet. A parse failure on fixed input isn't temporary; it's a verdict.

The classification question to ask before adding any retry: *what will be different on the next attempt?* If the honest answer is 'nothing', the retry is pure delay - and worse, it can mislead: five attempts in a log look like a struggling service rather than one bad input, sending whoever investigates toward the network instead of the form.

There's also a subtle cost: the retry loop caught `ValueError` broadly around the parse, so if the parser later gains a genuine bug that also raises `ValueError`, that bug gets retried-and-buried too. Retry the error *classes* that are transient by nature (timeouts, connection resets, 503s) and let verdicts like parse failures and validation errors end the matter on the first try.

Our payment call times out sometimes, and the natural instinct is 'just retry it'. But a timeout doesn't tell us whether the charge landed. Retrying blind double-charged a customer last month. How do we make the retry safe?

arguments.code:
# naive: a retry after a timeout charges again
charges = []
def charge_naive(amount):
    charges.append(amount)
    return "charged"

charge_naive(50)
charge_naive(50)   # the retry, after a timeout hid the first success
print("naive retry -> ledger:", charges)

# keyed: the caller attaches an idempotency key, reused on retry
ledger = []
seen_keys = set()
def charge(amount, key):
    if key in seen_keys:
        return "duplicate suppressed"
    seen_keys.add(key)
    ledger.append(amount)
    return "charged"

first = charge(50, "order-9")
second = charge(50, "order-9")   # same retry, same key
print("keyed retry -> first:", first + ", second:", second)
print("keyed ledger:", ledger, "total:", sum(ledger))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
naive retry -> ledger: [50, 50]
keyed retry -> first: charged, second: duplicate suppressed
keyed ledger: [50] total: 50

The timeout created an ambiguity: the charge may or may not have landed, and from the caller's side both worlds look identical. A blind retry resolves the ambiguity by gambling - and the naive ledger shows the losing ticket: the customer paid twice for one order.

The idempotency key dissolves the ambiguity instead of gambling on it. The caller generates one key per *logical* operation ('order-9's payment') and sends the same key on every retry. The receiver records keys it has already applied; a retry with a known key is acknowledged ('duplicate suppressed') without applying the effect again. The keyed ledger ends with exactly one 50 charge, which is the truth.

The design questions move to the right places: the key must be generated before the first attempt (a fresh key per retry defeats the whole scheme), stored by the receiver for at least as long as retries are possible, and scoped to the operation's identity, not the attempt. Before retrying any operation with side effects - charges, emails, shipments, inserts - the first question is never 'how many attempts' but 'what makes attempt two safe'. If nothing does, don't retry; reconcile instead.

I need a rule for which exceptions my service client should retry. Right now it's 'retry everything three times' and it feels wrong in both directions - too eager for some errors, maybe not enough for others.

Sort errors by what they *mean*, not by their position in a hierarchy:

**Retry - the failure is about timing or load, and the world may change:** timeouts, connection resets and refused connections, HTTP 502/503/504, 'database is locked', rate-limit responses (429 - and honor the Retry-After if one is given). These say 'not now', not 'never'.

**Never retry unchanged - the request itself is the problem:** validation errors, parse failures, 400/404/401/403, constraint violations. The identical request will earn the identical verdict. Retrying these only delays the inevitable and pollutes logs.

You're missing the second of two distinct layers:

**Structural validation** asks 'is this shaped like an order?' - valid JSON, required fields present, strings where strings belong, numbers where numbers belong. It's mechanical, schema-expressible, and it's the layer you have.

**Semantic validation** asks 'does this order make sense?' - quantities positive, delivery not before the order date, the discount not exceeding the price, the customer existing, the SKU being sellable. These rules live in your business, not in the data's shape, and no schema language will write them for you.

The failures you listed are all semantic: `-3` is a perfectly well-formed integer; '2026-01-01' is a perfectly well-formed date. Structure can't see them. Semantic checks also differ in kind: some are self-contained (quantity > 0), some are cross-field (date ordering, discount vs price), and some need the database (does this customer exist, is this SKU active) - which is why they belong in the service layer that has that access, right after structural parsing hands over typed values.

Order matters, too: run structure first (you can't compare dates that didn't parse), then field semantics, then cross-field, then referential. And report semantic failures as a collected list like form errors - the sender can usually fix several at once.
I want to collect all of a product's problems and report them together, but exceptions feel single-message-shaped. How do people carry a whole list of problems in one exception?

messages.content:
headline: 3 problem(s) found
  1. price must be positive, got -5
  2. sku is empty
  3. stock cannot be negative, got -2

The exception carries the list as an attribute - `e.problems` - while its message stays a one-line headline ('3 problem(s) found') for logs and tracebacks. The catcher gets both renderings: the headline for the log, the list for the user interface, which prints the numbered problems the merchant can work through in one pass.

This is the collect-all pattern packaged for transport across layers. The validator deep in the service layer accumulates; the exception is the envelope; whoever renders the response unpacks. Without the envelope you'd be reduced to joining problems into one long string at the raise site - and then the UI couldn't number them, translate them, or attach them to form fields without parsing your prose.

Keep the two parts in their lanes: `problems` holds the facts (one string per problem is fine at this scale; a list of small structured objects - field, rule, value - is the grown-up version), and the message stays a summary. If you find the message duplicating the whole list, the headline has stopped earning its place.
My required-field check is `if not value: raise MissingField`. A customer just set a quantity to 0 - a legitimate order of zero extra units - and got told the field is missing. Why did my check fire?

Because `not value` doesn't test for missing - it tests for *falsiness*, and Python's falsy family is bigger than 'absent': `None`, `''`, `0`, `0.0`, `[]`, and `False` are all falsy. Your check conflates three states that mean different things:

- **Missing**: the key isn't there, or the value is `None`. Test with `value is None` (after a `.get()` that returns None for absent keys).
- **Empty**: a string of nothing - `''`, or whitespace-only after `.strip()`. That's a string-specific test.
- **Zero**: a real, meaningful number. `0` is data, not absence - zero extra units, zero discount, a balance of exactly zero.

The string `'0'` makes the trap two-sided: it's *truthy* (non-empty string), so a text field containing zero passes `not value`, while the integer 0 fails it. The same logical quantity gets opposite verdicts depending on which side of parsing it sits - another argument for parsing at the boundary first, then validating the typed value.

Write the check you mean: `if value is None: raise MissingField` for presence, a separate emptiness check for strings, and range checks (`value < 0`) for numbers. Truthiness is a fine shortcut for 'is there anything in this collection to process' and a bug farm almost everywhere else.
My codebase validates the same fields in the handler, the service, and the repository - triple work, and the rules have drifted apart. Where does validation actually belong?

At the trust boundaries - the places where data passes from a world you don't control into the one you do. Concretely: user input at the request handler, file contents at the reader, network payloads at the client, environment variables and config at startup, and anything arriving from another service. Data crossing one of those lines gets parsed and validated *once*, at the crossing, into typed values your internals can trust.

Inside the boundary, functions should stop re-validating. When the service and the repository re-check what the handler already guaranteed, you pay three times: the code, the maintenance when a rule changes (your drift problem - three copies of a rule are three chances to update two), and the confusion of not knowing which layer's error a user will see. Internal functions can still *assert* their invariants as bug-catchers, but that's a different mechanism for a different audience.

Environment variables are the boundary people forget: `os.environ` values are always strings, supplied by whoever launched the process. Parse them once at startup into ints, booleans, and paths, and fail fast at boot with a message naming the variable - a misconfigured deploy should die in the first second, not on the first request.

The test for placement: if a value's badness would be *your caller's fault*, validate; if it would be *your own bug*, assert. Boundaries are where caller-fault lives.
Every field in this booking passes its individual check - guests is a number, the dates are dates, the discount is a number - and the booking is still nonsense. What kind of validation catches this?

messages.content:
- guests must be at least 1, got 0
- checkout 2026-12-09 must be after checkin 2026-12-10
- discount 350 exceeds price 300

Cross-field validation: rules about *relationships* between values. A checkout of 2026-12-09 is a perfectly valid date; a checkin of 2026-12-10 is a perfectly valid date; the booking is impossible because of how they stand to each other. No per-field check, however thorough, can express that - the rule needs both values in the room at once. Same for the discount exceeding the price: each number is plausible alone.

Structurally, these checks run after the per-field pass (comparing unparsed values is meaningless), over the whole record, and they belong in the same collected-problems report - the user experiences one booking with three problems, not two species of rejection.

ISO date strings are doing quiet work here: `YYYY-MM-DD` compares correctly as plain strings, which is one reason to normalize dates into ISO form at the boundary. With real `date` objects the comparisons are equally direct. Either way, the lesson stands: when a nonsense record passes every check you have, don't add more field checks - look for the relationship nobody is checking.

My registration code lets sqlite's IntegrityError bubble up to the web layer, which has no idea what to do with it. I want a domain error instead - but I don't want to lose the database's explanation. How do I translate without losing?

messages.content:
first registration ok
domain error: email already registered: ada@example.com
cause preserved: IntegrityError - UNIQUE constraint failed: users.email

The translation happens at the repository boundary - the one layer that speaks both languages. It catches sqlite's `IntegrityError` and raises `DuplicateEmail`, the concept the rest of your application actually thinks in. The web layer can now map `DuplicateEmail` to a 409 and a friendly message without importing sqlite or parsing SQL text.

And nothing is lost: `from e` attaches the original as `__cause__`, so the log still shows 'UNIQUE constraint failed: users.email' underneath your domain error. Translation is a change of vocabulary, not a destruction of evidence.

One discipline: translate the errors you *expect* and can name - a uniqueness violation on this insert means duplicate email. A blanket `except sqlite3.Error: raise MyError` would also translate disk failures and schema bugs into misleading domain errors. The narrower the catch, the more truthful the translation.
Our API returns whatever str(exception) happens to be, so clients can't programmatically tell a bad field from a missing resource from a server bug. What shape should error responses take?

messages.content:

The third case is the security lesson: the `RuntimeError`'s own text mentions an internal IP address, and the response deliberately replaces it with a generic message under the stable code 'internal'. The detail isn't destroyed - it belongs in your server log, keyed by a request id - but it is not the client's business.

Build this translation in exactly one place, at the API boundary, driven by exception *types*. If handlers throughout the codebase hand-assemble error dicts, the shape will drift per endpoint and clients are back to guessing.
My API basically returns 400 for every client problem and 500 for everything else. Reviewers keep mentioning 404, 409, and 422 as if the distinctions matter. Do they, and what's the rule?

They matter because clients act on them - retry logic, user messaging, and monitoring all key off the status. The distinctions, by what went wrong:

- **400 Bad Request** - the request couldn't be understood at all: malformed JSON, wrong types, unparseable syntax. The server never got to your meaning.
- **422 Unprocessable Entity** - the request parsed fine but breaks domain rules: end date before start date, discount over 100%, a well-formed email for a domain you don't serve. (Some APIs fold this into 400; pick one convention and be consistent - but 422 says 'your grammar was fine, your facts weren't'.)
- **404 Not Found** - the named resource doesn't exist: GET /users/99 when there is no user 99. Not for 'your search matched nothing' - an empty result set is a successful 200 with an empty list.
- **409 Conflict** - the request is valid but collides with current state: duplicate unique email, version mismatch on an optimistic-locked update, deleting something that has dependents. 409 tells the client 're-read the state and reconcile', which is a different instruction than 'fix your syntax'.
- **500 Internal Server Error** - *your* bug or your broken dependency, full stop. If a 500 can be produced by anything the client sent, the mapping is wrong - the client can't fix your NullPointerException, and paging your on-call for client typos trains everyone to ignore the pager.

The underlying rule: the status encodes *whose problem it is and what to do next* - fix the request (400/422), look elsewhere (404), reconcile with state (409), or wait while the server team works (500).

A security review flagged that our signup endpoint's error responses contain raw database messages. I didn't think a constraint message was sensitive. What exactly leaks, and what should the response be?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
leaky response would expose: UNIQUE constraint failed: accounts.email
translated response: {'status': 409, 'error': 'that email is already registered'}

The leaked string - 'UNIQUE constraint failed: accounts.email' - publishes three things: your table name, your column name, and your database's dialect. Individually small, but they're free reconnaissance for anyone probing the API, and they make the client parse SQL-flavored prose to learn what happened. Worse, the leak is unbounded: whatever the database says next time (a file path in a disk error, a query fragment) goes out the same door.

The translated response speaks the API's own vocabulary: status 409 (a state conflict, which is what a duplicate is) and a sentence about the *user's* situation, not your schema. The database's message still exists - in your server log, attached as the cause - where it helps you and exposes nothing.

The general principle is that each layer's errors are written in that layer's language. The moment one layer's raw error crosses another layer's boundary untranslated, you've coupled your clients to your internals and your security posture to your database's verbosity.
My API returns 404 when a search finds no users, and also 404 when a specific user id doesn't exist. A client developer says one of those is wrong and it's breaking her code. Which one, and why?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
get existing: Ada
get missing -> 404: user 99
search with no matches -> 200 with: []

The search is the wrong one. The two operations ask different questions. `get_user(99)` names one specific resource and asserts it should be there - its absence is an error condition, and 404 is the honest answer. `search_users` asks for a *set* matching a filter; an empty set is a complete, successful answer to that question, so it returns 200 with `[]`.

Your client developer's breakage is concrete: her code likely treats 404 as 'the thing is gone, show the missing page / stop retrying' - and a search that legitimately matches nothing triggers that path, making 'no results' indistinguishable from 'the endpoint moved'. Conversely, if a single-resource get returned 200-with-null for missing ids, clients would render phantom users.

Notice how the code enforces the distinction: `get_user` translates a `KeyError` into a domain `NotFound`, while `search_users` has no error path at all for the empty case - emptiness is in its return type. When the semantics differ, the signatures should differ; don't make one function (or one status code) carry both meanings.

My import pipeline has three stages - ingest, validate, store - and when it fails, the error doesn't say which stage died, so the on-call has to reproduce the run to find out. How do I make failures self-locating?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
pipeline error: stage 'store' failed: batch total 140 exceeds limit 100
stage: store | root cause: ValueError - batch total 140 exceeds limit 100

Each stage boundary wraps whatever escapes with the stage's name, and the original rides along as `__cause__`. The on-call now reads 'stage 'store' failed' and the root cause in one line - no reproduction needed to know whether to call the data team (ingest/validate) or the storage team.

Two design points. The wrap is *uniform*: `run_stage` applies it to every stage, so no stage can forget and leak a bare error - uniformity is what makes the tag trustworthy. And the tag is data (the `stage` attribute), not just prose, so dashboards can count failures per stage and alert on the one that spikes.

The catch in `run_stage` is broad (`Exception`) and that's legitimate here - this is a boundary whose entire job is annotation, and it re-raises rather than swallowing. Annotating boundaries are one of the few places a broad catch adds information instead of destroying it - provided, as here, the original is always chained, never replaced.

I get contradictory advice: 'translate errors as low as possible' versus 'let them bubble to the boundary'. In my app the database errors sometimes reach the HTTP layer raw, and other times get wrapped so early that the service layer can't tell a disk failure from a duplicate key. Where's the line?

Translate at the point where the *vocabulary* changes - which is the boundary of the component that owns the lower-level tool. Your repository owns sqlite, so the repository is where `IntegrityError` becomes `DuplicateEmail`: it's the last layer that understands SQL and the first that understands your domain.

Your two failure modes are the symmetric mistakes:

- **Too late (raw leak):** above the repository, nobody should know sqlite exists. If the HTTP layer can see an `IntegrityError`, it must either leak it or grow SQL knowledge - both are coupling. The repository failed to do its translation job.
- **Too early (over-translation):** if the repository wraps *every* `sqlite3.Error` into one generic `StorageError`, it destroys the distinctions the service layer needs - a uniqueness violation (user's fault, 409) and a disk-full (nobody's fault, page someone) become the same error. Translation must be *selective*: catch the specific low-level errors whose meaning you know, translate those, and let the rest propagate unchanged (or chained under a genuinely generic wrapper that doesn't pretend to know what happened).

A useful test per layer boundary: 'Can every error that crosses this line be described in the vocabulary of the layer above, without lying?' Duplicates: yes. Disk failures: they cross as infrastructure errors, honestly labeled as such - not dressed as domain errors. The line isn't a depth in the stack; it's the edge of each tool's ownership.

Two editors can open the same document in my app. We use optimistic locking - each save includes the version the editor saw - but when versions clash, the loser's save just... does nothing, silently, and they think their edit saved. Where does the failure signal get lost?

arguments.code:
import sqlite3

class ConflictError(Exception):
    pass

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE docs (id INTEGER, body TEXT, version INTEGER)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO docs VALUES (1, 'draft', 3)")

def update_doc(doc_id, body, expected_version):
    cur = db.execute(
        "UPDATE docs SET body = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?",
        (body, doc_id, expected_version))
    if cur.rowcount == 0:
        raise ConflictError(f"doc {doc_id} was modified by someone else")
    return "updated"

print("first editor:", update_doc(1, "revised", 3))
try:
    update_doc(1, "my overwrite", 3)   # second editor still holds version 3
except ConflictError as e:
    print("second editor -> 409:", e)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
first editor: updated
second editor -> 409: doc 1 was modified by someone else

The signal was there all along - `rowcount` - and nobody was reading it. The version-guarded UPDATE is designed to match zero rows when the document has moved on; that's the mechanism working, not failing. But a zero-row UPDATE raises nothing, so if the code doesn't check, the no-op is indistinguishable from success, and the second editor walks away believing 'my overwrite' is saved when it never touched the database.

The repository's job is to convert that silent outcome into an explicit error: `rowcount == 0` after a guarded update means exactly one thing - someone else saved first - so it raises `ConflictError`, which the API layer maps to 409 with a 'reload and merge' message. The editor now gets the truth while their text is still on screen.

Generalize the pattern: any operation whose failure mode is 'nothing happened' - a guarded update, a conditional delete, a compare-and-swap - must have its effect *counted* and the zero case raised. Silence is only acceptable when nothing happening was a legitimate success.
We're writing the error-handling section of our API contract for external developers. What should we promise them about errors - and what should we be careful never to promise?

Promise structure, not prose. External developers build on your errors, so the contract should fix:

- **The envelope**: every error response has the same shape - an HTTP status, a stable machine-readable `code` string, a human `message`, and where relevant a `field` or a request id for support lookups.
- **The code list**: the finite set of codes and what each means, with the commitment that codes are never reused for a different meaning. Developers will switch on these; renaming one is a breaking change, so treat the list like your endpoint list.
- **The retry semantics per code**: which codes are worth retrying (transient ones) and which are verdicts. This one paragraph will save your support queue a thousand tickets.

What never to promise: the exact wording of `message`. Messages are for humans and you will improve them, translate them, and fix their typos; if a developer parses them, that's the string-matching trap, and your contract should say explicitly 'messages may change; codes are the contract'.

And the boundary of the whole document: internal detail never crosses. No exception class names, no SQL text, no stack frames, no hostnames - not because developers are adversaries, but because anything you publish becomes a dependency and a disclosure at once. The request id is the bridge: the client quotes it, your logs hold the full internal story under that key.

We call a vendor SDK for shipping labels, and its exception types - SdkTimeout, SdkAuth, SdkBadAddress, a dozen more - have leaked into every layer of our code. Swapping vendors someday would mean touching everything. How do I contain them?

Build exactly one doorway. All SDK calls go through a single wrapper module whose job includes translating the vendor's errors into *your* taxonomy - the small set of distinctions your application actually acts on:

- `SdkTimeout`, connection errors → your `TransientError` (caller may retry)
- `SdkAuth` → your `ConfigurationError` (don't retry; page a human, credentials are wrong)
- `SdkBadAddress` → your `InvalidShipment` carrying the field that failed (the user's problem, show it to them)
- Anything unrecognized → your `VendorError`, chained from the original

Every translation uses `raise Mine(...) from e`, so the vendor's detail survives in logs as the cause while your service layer catches only your types. The dozen vendor types collapse to the four decisions your code actually makes - retry, escalate, show the user, or give up - which is the real taxonomy; the vendor's finer distinctions were *their* internals, not your decisions.

Then enforce the doorway: no other module imports the SDK. A lint rule or a code-review habit ('the SDK package may only be imported in shipping/client.py') keeps it true. When the vendor swap comes, you rewrite one module's translations and the rest of the codebase never learns the new vendor's exception names - which is the entire point.
I use assert for everything - checking inputs, checking my own logic. A reviewer said asserts are for one of those jobs and actively wrong for the other. Which is which?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
([2, 4, 6], [1, 3, 5])
empty input -> real exception: ages must not be empty

The assert in `partition` guards a fact about *the function's own work*: splitting a list into evens and odds must conserve the count. If that assert ever fires, the bug is in `partition` - no input can make it fire, because every integer is even or odd. That's the assert's proper job: a tripwire over your own reasoning, addressed to you, the programmer.

The empty-list check in `average_age` is the opposite situation: empty input is something a *caller* can legitimately hand you, and the response is a real `ValueError` with a message - catchable, typed, and present in every run mode. If that check were an assert, the caller would get a bare `AssertionError` (which reads as 'the library is broken', not 'your input is') - and, as the next examples show, asserts can be switched off entirely.

The sorting question for any check: 'Whose fault would a violation be?' If the answer is 'mine, the author's' - assert. If it's 'whoever supplied this value' - raise a proper exception. Input validation, authorization, and anything the outside world controls belong to the second kind, always.

program = (
    "def set_level(n):\n"
    "    assert 0 <= n <= 10, 'level out of range'\n"
    "    return n\n"
    "print('set_level(99) ->', set_level(99))\n"
)

for flags in ([], ["-O"]):
    p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, *flags, "-c", program],
                       capture_output=True, text=True)

flags=['(none)']: exit 1, last line: AssertionError: level out of range
flags=['-O']: exit 0, last line: set_level(99) -> 99

It's real. The `-O` flag (and the `PYTHONOPTIMIZE` environment variable) puts the interpreter in optimized mode, in which `assert` statements are not compiled at all - they vanish from the bytecode. Watch the two runs of the *identical* program: normally, `set_level(99)` dies with `AssertionError: level out of range`, exit code 1. Under `-O`, the guard isn't there - the function returns 99 and the program exits 0, printing success.

Nothing warned, nothing logged. The validation didn't fail; it ceased to exist. And the person who deploys your code controls this flag, not you - a Docker image, a systemd unit, or a well-meaning performance tweak can set it without your knowledge.

This is the mechanical reason behind the rule 'never validate with assert'. It's not that asserts are weak in normal runs - it's that their existence is conditional on a deployment setting. Any check whose absence would let bad data through, skip an authorization, or corrupt state must be an `if` with a `raise`, which no flag can remove.
Give me the simple rule for assert vs raise that I can put on the team wiki - including why, in one or two sentences each, so people actually follow it.

Here it is, in wiki form:

**Use `assert` for facts about your own code.** An assert says 'if this is ever false, *I* have a bug'. It guards invariants - the partition conserves elements, the cache key matches the value, the state machine is in a legal state. Its audience is the programmer, its firing means 'stop and fix the code', and it may legitimately be compiled away in optimized runs because production input can never trigger it.

**Use `raise` for facts about the outside world.** A raise says 'whoever supplied this value broke the contract'. It validates inputs, enforces permissions, and rejects impossible requests - anything a user, a file, a network peer, or another team's service can influence. Its audience is the caller, it carries a type and a message the caller can act on, and it exists in every run mode because the outside world doesn't care about your optimizer flags.

**The one-line test**: 'Could this check ever fire because of something outside this process's control?' Yes → raise. No, only if my code is wrong → assert.

Post that, and review for the two classic violations: asserts checking user input (validation that can vanish), and hand-rolled `if ...: raise AssertionError` for internal invariants (crash reports that blame the caller for your bug).
Our crash reports from production just say 'AssertionError' and a file and line. Half the time I open the file and still can't tell what value broke the assumption. Are assert messages worth writing?

Yes - an assert's message is the difference between a tripwire and a riddle. A bare `assert total == expected` tells the reader *that* an equality failed; `assert total == expected, f'total {total} != expected {expected} after discounts'` tells them by how much and in which phase - often enough to identify the bug without reproducing anything.

Write the values, not a restatement of the condition. The condition is already in the source at the line the report names; what the source can't give the reader is the *runtime state* - the two totals, the unexpected state name, the id being processed. That state exists only at the moment of failure, and the message is your one chance to capture it.

Two refinements. In tests, bare asserts are fine and idiomatic - pytest rewrites them and prints the compared values itself, which is the tooling doing this job for you. That convenience ends at the test boundary: production asserts get no rewriting, so the message discipline is yours. And keep messages cheap: an f-string on an assert costs nothing when the assert passes (it's only evaluated on failure), so there's no performance excuse for a bare one on any assert whose failure you'd actually want to diagnose.
